whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is a complete sentence: "It was the kind of challenge that would set any art curator's mind into motion." What follows — "finding that elusive thread that could link artists as disparate as..." — is not a sentence; it names what the challenge actually was. A colon is the mark that lets a complete sentence introduce an explanation or specification like that, so "motion: finding" is the only version that punctuates the two parts correctly.

whyWrong.A: Puts the colon after "finding" instead of before it, so the colon interrupts "finding" from its own object, "that elusive thread" — a colon can never separate a verb from what it acts on.
whyWrong.B: A period demands a complete sentence on each side, and "Finding that elusive thread that could link artists..." has no main verb; it is a fragment.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon joins two independent clauses, but the material after the blank is a participial phrase, not a clause that could stand alone.

commonMistakes: Assuming any of the four marks will do because the phrase after the blank is long; length has nothing to do with it — only whether each side can stand alone.
tips: Test the words after the blank on their own: if they cannot be a sentence, a period and a semicolon are both out, which usually leaves the colon.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with "Currently," which fixes the time frame as right now, and describing a species' present-day range calls for the simple present. "Includes" is the only choice in that tense, and it agrees with the singular subject "the frog's range."

whyWrong.A: The present perfect "has included" describes something that began earlier and continues, which conflicts with "Currently" pointing at the present moment alone.
whyWrong.B: The future perfect "will have included" places the action before some later point in the future — nothing in the text sets up a future reference point.
whyWrong.D: The simple past "included" says the range was that way at some finished earlier time, contradicting "Currently."

tips: When a sentence hands you a time marker like "Currently," "In 1902," or "By next year," match the verb to that marker before you look at anything else.

whyCorrect: Look at what comes after the comma: "both the Orden Hijos de América (1921) and the Partido Nacional de La Raza Unida (1970) contributed to the history of US civil rights" is a complete sentence with its own subject and verb. "The 20th century saw the founding of many Latino advocacy groups" is also a complete sentence. Two complete sentences cannot be joined by a comma, so the blank has to end the first one with a period. That leaves "Established to protect and advance the rights of Latino Americans" as an opening participial phrase modifying the two organizations that follow it.

whyWrong.A: "and established" makes "the 20th century" the thing that established something, and it still leaves a comma splice before "both the Orden..."
whyWrong.B: Attaching "established to protect..." to "groups" keeps the first half a complete sentence, so the comma before "both the Orden..." joins two independent clauses — a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: Same splice as B; adding a comma after "groups" changes only how the modifier is set off, not the illegal comma joining the two sentences.

commonMistakes: Choosing based on how the modifier sounds next to "groups" without checking that the second half of the sentence is independent.

whyCorrect: The end of the text — "the method emphasizes learning from skilled musicians... and teaches students as young as three..." — is a full sentence with its own subject, "the method." So the words before it must be a separate sentence, and the only complete one available is "The pedagogy of the Suzuki method is rooted in several central tenets." A period at the blank does that, and "Developed by Japanese violinist Shinichi Suzuki, who sought to parallel the linguistic learning environment," then works as an opening modifier describing the method.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, "tenets developed by... Suzuki, who sought to parallel the linguistic learning environment, the method emphasizes..." runs one complete sentence straight into another.
whyWrong.B: A comma after "tenets" still leaves two independent clauses joined only by commas — a splice, not a fix.
whyWrong.D: "tenets that, developed by..." starts a relative clause with "that" and then never gives it a verb, so the clause is left dangling.

tips: Find the sentence's real main verb first — here it is "emphasizes" — then check whether the words before it can stand alone.

whyCorrect: "The Serna v. Portales Schools court decision in 1974, which affirmed the rights of Latino students, is another such event" is a complete sentence, so the words before it must end with a period, not a comma. Putting "for one" at the end of the first sentence also keeps it attached to the right thing: El Teatro Campesino is the "one" example, and the Serna decision is then "another."

whyWrong.A: Joins two complete sentences with only a comma after "for one" — a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: Same comma splice, and it also drops the comma that should set off "for one" as an interrupter.
whyWrong.D: Grammatically it ends the sentence, but it moves "For one" onto the Serna decision, which the same sentence calls "another such event" — you cannot introduce something as both the first example and an additional one.

commonMistakes: Treating this as a pure punctuation question and stopping once you find an option that ends the first sentence; here you also have to see which side "for one" belongs on.

whyCorrect: "The gaseous compounds" on its own does not tell you which compounds, so the names "thymol and methane" are essential information and take no commas around them. Once you drop the commas, nothing separates the subject "the gaseous compounds thymol and methane" from its verb "have," which is exactly what Standard English requires.

whyWrong.A: Opens a nonessential element with a comma after "compounds" but never closes it before "have," leaving the punctuation unpaired.
whyWrong.B: Pairs the commas correctly but marks the names as nonessential, which would mean the sentence already identifies the compounds without them — it does not.
whyWrong.D: Places a single comma between the complete subject and the verb "have," which is never allowed.

tips: Ask whether the noun phrase before the names already points to something specific; if it does not, the names are essential and get no commas.

whyCorrect: The two sentences are events in sequence: Gomez won a competition in 2014, and then in 2017 he created a show. The transition only needs to mark that the second event came after the first, which is what "Later" does.

whyWrong.A: "Instead" signals that the second thing replaced the first, but creating the show did not take the place of winning the competition.
whyWrong.B: "For example" would make the show an instance of winning a storytelling competition, and it is not — it is a separate thing he founded.
whyWrong.D: "In other words" introduces a restatement of the same idea, but the second sentence gives new information rather than rephrasing the first.

tips: When both sentences carry dates, check whether the relationship is just chronological before reaching for a fancier transition.

whyCorrect: The clause before the semicolon says what Chaucer did not write in, and the clause after it supplies the correct alternative. That negation-then-correction pattern calls for "rather," which means "instead, the truth is this."

whyWrong.B: "Finally" marks the last item in a sequence, but nothing here is being listed in order.
whyWrong.C: "As a result" claims the second clause is caused by the first; writing Middle English is not an effect of not writing Modern English, it is the same fact stated positively.
whyWrong.D: "Similarly" signals a parallel between two like things, but the two clauses contrast a denial with a correction.

tips: A negative statement followed by the accurate version almost always takes "rather" or "instead."

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank gives one reason Honeoye suits the role of state soil — it is abundant. The sentence after gives a second, separate reason — it supports agriculture. Adding a reason on top of a reason calls for an additive transition, which is "Moreover."

whyWrong.A: "At that time" points back to a specific moment already named, and the passage never establishes one.
whyWrong.B: "Alternatively" offers a competing option, but the agricultural role does not replace or compete with the abundance point.
whyWrong.C: "Conversely" signals a reversal, yet both sentences argue the same way — that Honeoye is a fitting state soil.

commonMistakes: Picking a contrast word because the second sentence introduces something new; new is not the same as opposed.

whyCorrect: The goal is to state one element's relative abundance on Earth, so the sentence has to name an element, name Earth, and give the actual figure. Only the potassium sentence does all three by reporting its mass fraction as a percentage on Earth. The other choices describe how abundance can be measured, or compare two elements, without ever stating a value.

whyWrong.A: Lists the three ways abundance can be expressed; it never gives any element's abundance on Earth.
whyWrong.C: Says potassium's abundance can be expressed three ways but withholds the number, so nothing is specified.
whyWrong.D: Compares two elements rather than specifying an abundance, and the comparison contradicts the notes — potassium's 0.016% is far smaller than calcium's 1.71%.

tips: Turn the stated goal into a checklist of the pieces the sentence must contain, then eliminate anything missing a piece.

whyCorrect: The goal is a similarity, so the sentence has to mention both artifacts and state something they share. Only this choice names the spoon and the purse together and points to what is true of each — both sit in the Hina Hanta archive and both are Choctaw cultural artifacts.

whyWrong.A: Mentions only the spoon, so there is no second item to be similar to.
whyWrong.C: Uses the 1949 date to draw a distinction about dates rather than a shared trait, and the spoon appears only by implication.
whyWrong.D: Frames the two artifacts as different in age, which is a contrast, the opposite of what the goal asks for.

tips: For a "similarity" goal, require both subjects in the sentence and a shared property — a date comparison is a contrast even when both items appear.

whyCorrect: A similarity sentence needs both positions plus a trait they hold in common. The notes say first position and demi-seconde position are each a position for the dancer's arms, and that is the one thing the notes state about both. This choice names both and gives exactly that shared feature.

whyWrong.B: Misstates the notes: first position belongs to the Vaganova method, not the Royal Academy of Dance.
whyWrong.C: Names both positions but its "in contrast to" wording sets them against each other, emphasizing the difference in arm placement.
whyWrong.D: Talks only about Vaganova and first position, so no comparison of any kind is made.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option that mentions both positions without checking whether it links them as alike or as different.

whyCorrect: The second sentence is the definition of the blank: scholars "inadvertently overlook nuances" when they focus on the obvious transcendentalist features. The blank needs a word meaning to treat subtleties as unimportant or to disregard them, and "discount" is exactly that.

whyWrong.A: "Magnify" means to make subtleties more prominent, the reverse of overlooking them.
whyWrong.B: "Scrutinize" means to examine closely, which is what the scholars fail to do with the nuances.
whyWrong.D: "Denounce" means to condemn publicly, an attack on the subtleties rather than a failure to notice them.

tips: When the next sentence starts with "for instance," it is usually restating the blank in plainer words — read it first.

whyCorrect: The phrase after the dash explains the blank: she is "drawing from memories of her childhood" and "details of her current surroundings." Drawing on lived experience to make art is being inspired by it, and the sentence's structure — no matter what she creates, this is always her source — points to a positive, sourcing relationship.

whyWrong.A: "Complimented by" means praised by someone; direct experience does not pay compliments, and praise is not what the memories provide.
whyWrong.B: "Uncertain about" contradicts the rest of the sentence, which shows her drawing confidently on specific memories and surroundings.
whyWrong.C: "Unbothered by" would mean experience does not affect her, but the sentence says it is the thing she works from.

commonMistakes: Confusing "complimented" (praised) with "complemented" (completed); even the latter would not fit the idea of drawing material from memory.

whyCorrect: The second sentence says Demosthenes repeatedly argued in public addresses that parrhesia was the very foundation of Athenian democracy — that is, he publicly argued for its value. Someone who publicly advocates an idea is a proponent of it.

whyWrong.B: "A steward" manages or safeguards something entrusted to him; the text shows him arguing for an idea, not administering it.
whyWrong.C: "An apprentice" is a beginner learning a trade under a master, which does not describe a prominent orator championing a principle.
whyWrong.D: "A harbinger" is a sign that something is coming, but parrhesia was already practiced in Athens and Demosthenes was defending it, not foreshadowing it.

tips: Match the blank to the evidence verb — here "characterizing... as the foundation of democracy" in "public addresses" is advocacy.

whyCorrect: "Good" here modifies "height," a measurement, not a person's character. The clause that follows — his height could be judged "even from the seated figure" — tells you he is notably tall, so "good" means large in amount. "Considerable" is the sense of "good" used in phrases like "a good distance" or "a good while."

whyWrong.A: "Well-behaved" describes conduct, and a height cannot behave.
whyWrong.C: "Capable" describes a person's ability; it cannot modify a measurement.
whyWrong.D: "Reliable" would mean the height can be counted on, which makes no sense as a description of stature.

tips: Check what the word actually modifies before choosing a meaning — a common sense of the word applied to the wrong noun is the usual trap.

whyCorrect: The colon means the second half of the sentence restates the hypothesis: the more work people believe went into a piece, the more they appreciate it. That is a statement that effort raises a work's worth in their eyes, so the blank needs a verb meaning to prize or place worth on. "Value" is that verb.

whyWrong.B: "Perform" would mean the viewers themselves do the labor, but the effort described belongs to the artist.
whyWrong.C: "Prevent" makes viewers stop the effort from happening, which has nothing to do with how much they appreciate the result.
whyWrong.D: "Neglect" means to disregard the effort, the opposite of appreciating a piece more when more work went into it.

tips: A colon promises a restatement — read the clause after it and put its idea into one verb before looking at the choices.

whyCorrect: The claim has two parts: contemporary elements show up in modern A Midsummer Night's Dream productions, and they get there unintentionally. Only this quotation has a designer who was actively trying for period accuracy and only later recognized the 1980s fashion that had crept into the designs — deliberate effort at accuracy plus unnoticed contemporary influence is exactly the unintentional case.

whyWrong.A: Describes attention to period-appropriate accessories with no contemporary element and no mention of the play in question.
whyWrong.B: Names the play but describes flexibility that is chosen on purpose to communicate an idea, which makes the anachronism intentional, not accidental.
whyWrong.C: Argues that costumes should always match the period and criticizes period mixing; it prescribes a standard rather than reporting an unintentional lapse.

commonMistakes: Selecting the choice that merely mentions A Midsummer Night's Dream; the play title alone does not address the "unintentionally" half of the claim.

whyCorrect: The claim is specific: the speaker urges John to look for a relationship with someone else instead of waiting on her. This stanza names other women who might have him, tells him to ask them, and explicitly says not to stay single on her account — both halves of the claim in four lines.

whyWrong.A: Denies that she ever loved him and complains about being pestered, but points him toward no one else.
whyWrong.C: Offers friendship in place of love; it refuses him without suggesting he pursue another relationship.
whyWrong.D: Proposes that they be friends and drop hidden hopes, which again is about their own relationship, not about John seeking someone new.

tips: When the claim has two elements, keep both in mind — several choices will satisfy one of them.

whyCorrect: The claim is that Helena works to reduce the friction between Vanya and the professor. This quotation has her speaking directly to Vanya about the damage done by hate and spiteful tattling and telling him it is his duty to make peace with Serebrakoff — an explicit attempt to defuse the conflict.

whyWrong.A: Shows Helena complaining about her own exhaustion with the professor, which reveals her feelings rather than any peacemaking.
whyWrong.B: Pushes back against how others pity her; she is defending her marriage, not smoothing things between the two men.
whyWrong.D: Is spoken to Sonia about Helena's own unhappiness and never touches the Vanya-professor conflict.

commonMistakes: Picking any quotation in which Helena mentions her husband; the claim requires her to be acting on the conflict, not describing her own state.

whyCorrect: Chain the two studies together. Tarabieh: as perceived environmental risk goes up, likelihood of buying goes down — so lower perceived risk means higher likelihood of buying. The Vietnam study found parents of small children perceived the lowest environmental risk in the skin-care product of any group. Applying Tarabieh's relationship, that lowest risk perception should translate into the highest purchase likelihood, so those parents are the group most likely to buy it.

whyWrong.A: Introduces priorities that neither study measured; the finding is about how much risk parents perceived, not about what they weigh against sustainability.
whyWrong.B: Claims the groups are alike, but the second study explicitly reports parents of small children as the extreme low end of risk perception.
whyWrong.C: Reverses the direction — lower perceived risk predicts more appeal, not less — and compares the product with rival products the studies never examined.

tips: Write the first study as a direction (more risk perceived, less buying), then plug the second study's group into it before reading the choices.

whyCorrect: Desai's cross-country result says that strong democracy paired with low inequality restrains inflation. Austria has exactly that pairing, yet its 2017 inflation was higher than Cameroon's. If Austria's political structure should have pushed its inflation down and it was still the higher of the two, then that structure cannot be what produced the gap — something else about 2017 must account for it.

whyWrong.B: Credits inequality differences with most of the gap, but under Desai's finding Austria's low inequality should have lowered its inflation, not raised it above Cameroon's.
whyWrong.C: Questions the indices' accuracy, which nothing in the text does; Desai's study takes measured democratic strength as given and changes the interpretation, not the measurement.
whyWrong.D: Endorses the very critique Desai's result undercuts — that diluted state control drives inflation up — and it also speculates about a scenario the study never tested.

commonMistakes: Reading the Austria-Cameroon pair as evidence for the critique and then choosing an option that agrees with it; the sentence's "but" signals that Desai's finding overrides that first impression.

whyCorrect: "Olga Shurchkov of Wellesley College studies worker productivity" and "other researchers investigate areas such as market behavior and consumer behavior" are both complete sentences, so they need a semicolon between them, not a comma. "For instance" belongs to the first clause — Shurchkov is the example of the "variety of topics" — and as an interrupter at the end of that clause it takes a comma before it.

whyWrong.A: Places the semicolon correctly but drops the comma that must set off "for instance" from "productivity."
whyWrong.C: Attaches "for instance" to the second clause, which would present "other researchers investigate market behavior" as an example of Shurchkov studying productivity — it is a separate case, not an instance of it.
whyWrong.D: Uses commas on both sides, so two independent clauses end up joined by a comma: a comma splice.

tips: Decide which clause the interrupter modifies before you decide where the semicolon goes; both questions have to be answered together.

whyCorrect: "He did not play drums on the label's classic song 'Rapper's Delight'" and "he joined the label after the song's release" are both complete sentences, so a comma alone cannot join them. "However" belongs to the first clause: it contrasts with the previous sentence, which says Chambers is best known as Sugar Hill's house drummer. Ending that clause with ", however" and then using a semicolon links the statement to the explanation that follows.

whyWrong.A: Leaves two independent clauses joined by a comma; "however" is an adverb and cannot do a conjunction's work.
whyWrong.C: Punctuates correctly but moves "However" onto the second clause, making joining the label a contrast with not playing on the song — the second clause is the reason for the first, not a reversal of it.
whyWrong.D: Gives no punctuation at all between the two clauses and no comma around "however," producing a run-on.

commonMistakes: Assuming "however" always opens the second sentence; it just as often closes the first, and here the contrast points backward.

whyCorrect: Look at the end of the text: "2008 FC76, showing no such activity, is considered dormant" is the main clause, and "the object 2060 Chiron is considered an active centaur, showing sporadic comet-like activity" is a second complete clause sitting right before it with only a comma between them. Adding "while" turns the Chiron clause into a subordinate clause, which fixes that splice, and the colon lets the complete sentence ending in "behavior" introduce the two-part explanation of what those differences are.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon after "behavior" is legal, but with no "while" the Chiron clause and the FC76 clause remain two sentences joined by a comma.
whyWrong.B: Same problem as A — the period fixes one boundary and leaves the comma splice between the two centaur descriptions untouched.
whyWrong.D: Adds "while" but only a comma after "behavior," so "they exhibit striking differences in behavior, while the object 2060 Chiron is considered an active centaur" reads as a finished sentence and the FC76 clause is spliced on.

tips: Count the independent clauses in the whole sentence, not just around the blank — this one has a second boundary problem further along.

whyCorrect: "Compiled" is the verb and "climate data from several sites in Puerto Rico's Luquillo Mountains" is its direct object. Nothing may come between a verb and its object, so the blank takes no punctuation at all.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must have an independent clause on each side, and "climate data from several sites..." is only a noun phrase.
whyWrong.B: A colon must follow a complete sentence, but "researchers... compiled" breaks off before the verb has an object.
whyWrong.D: A comma here separates the verb from the object it acts on, which Standard English does not allow.

commonMistakes: Reading the long list of names as a signal that punctuation is needed; the names are the subject and the sentence still runs straight into its verb and object.

whyCorrect: "Okinaka doesn't make such decisions single-handedly" and "all historical designations must be approved by a group of nine other experts" are both complete sentences. "However" is an adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot join them — it can only sit inside one of them. Ending the first sentence with "single-handedly, however." and starting a new sentence with "All" is the only option that gives each clause its own sentence.

whyWrong.A: Produces the classic comma splice: two independent clauses with only "however" and commas between them.
whyWrong.B: "and" needs a comma before it to join two independent clauses, and "however and" stacks two connectives that do opposite jobs.
whyWrong.C: Runs the two sentences together with no punctuation and leaves "however" unmarked.

tips: Treat "however," "therefore," and "moreover" as adverbs that cannot glue two sentences together no matter how many commas surround them.

whyCorrect: The sentence has a subject — "emulsifiers such as stearyl alcohol" — but no main verb until the blank supplies one. "Are employed" is a finite verb in the passive voice, plural to match "emulsifiers," and it lets the infinitive "to blend oil and water" state the purpose.

whyWrong.A: "Employed" alone is a past participle here with no helping verb, so the sentence is left without a working main verb.
whyWrong.B: "Being employed" is a participle phrase, not a finite verb; the sentence never reaches a predicate.
whyWrong.D: "That they employ" starts a relative clause and reverses the roles, making the emulsifiers the ones doing the employing, and it still leaves the sentence without a main verb.

tips: Find the subject, then ask whether the sentence ever gets a verb that could carry tense; an -ing or bare -ed form cannot.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank says Montaigne constantly questions his own perspective. The sentence after gives his motto, "What do I know?" — a question that does exactly that. The motto suits the habit, so the transition needs to signal appropriateness, which is what "Fittingly" does.

whyWrong.A: "Still" concedes a point despite something previously said, but the motto reinforces the previous sentence rather than pushing against it.
whyWrong.B: "Conversely" announces an opposite, and a self-questioning motto is not the opposite of a habit of self-questioning.
whyWrong.D: "Nowadays" contrasts the present with the past, but both sentences describe Montaigne in his own time.

tips: When the second sentence is an illustration that matches the first perfectly, look for a word meaning "appropriately" before considering contrast words.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank states Brown's general claim — ornaments can serve a purpose. The sentence after names one such purpose: communicating information about a city's history and culture. That is a specific case of the general claim, so the transition must introduce an example.

whyWrong.A: "However" sets up a contrast, but the second sentence supports Brown's claim instead of qualifying it.
whyWrong.B: "As a result" makes the communicating a consequence of Brown's argument; it is an instance of what she argued, not an effect of her arguing it.
whyWrong.D: "Finally" closes a list, and no earlier purposes have been given for this one to conclude.

commonMistakes: Choosing "However" because the passage contains a disagreement between Loos and Brown; that contrast happens one sentence earlier, not at the blank.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes a place — India. The second gives a production figure but never names where it applies, so the transition has to supply that link. "There" means "in India," attaching the 18.8 million metric tons to the country just named.

whyWrong.A: "Hence" claims the production figure follows logically from one mango variety originating in India, which it does not.
whyWrong.C: "In fact" intensifies or confirms the previous statement, but the production total does not confirm where the Cheruku rasamu comes from.
whyWrong.D: "Specifically" narrows a general statement to a precise case, yet the second sentence is about total national output, not a narrower detail about that one variety.

tips: When the second sentence is missing a place or time that the first sentence supplies, the transition is doing locating work, not logical work.

whyCorrect: The goal is narrow: give an example of a film Prieto worked on. That means the sentence has to name Prieto and name a film. Only this choice does both, identifying Frida (2002) as a film he shot.

whyWrong.A: Names Prieto and a director but never names a film, so no example of a film is given.
whyWrong.C: Describes filmmaking in general and mentions neither Prieto nor any film.
whyWrong.D: Explains what a cinematographer does; it names Prieto but no particular film.

tips: When the goal says "provide an example of X," the sentence must actually contain an X — here, a film title.

whyCorrect: An objective is what the study set out to do. The notes state it directly: a primary aim was to determine the benefits of UNAs in these cities. This choice reports that aim as the point of the sentence, which is what "emphasize an objective" asks for.

whyWrong.A: Gives the study's duration and location — facts about how it was run, not what it was trying to find out.
whyWrong.B: Mentions an objective only in a subordinate opener and then makes the sentence about what was examined, so the emphasis lands on the forty-four types of UNAs.
whyWrong.D: Reports a benefit of large urban parks, which is a finding about the subject matter rather than a goal of the study.

commonMistakes: Accepting a sentence that merely contains the word "objective"; check what the main clause is actually about.

whyCorrect: The notes are about a 2019 Oahu study of seed dispersal, and the sentence that best represents the study presents both what the researchers did — catalogued seeds in bird fecal samples — and why they did it: to learn what role non-native birds play in dispersing seeds. The other choices report isolated details about individual plant species instead of the study itself.

whyWrong.A: States a background fact about Oahu's plants and reduces the study to nothing; it also treats one catalogued species as evidence for "most" species.
whyWrong.B: Compares the native status of two plants, a detail from the notes that says nothing about the study's work or purpose.
whyWrong.D: Lists two species found in the samples but omits the reason the researchers were looking, so the study's aim disappears.

commonMistakes: This item's goal sentence does not match its notes — it asks about the order in which supercontinents formed, which nothing in the notes concerns — so judge the choices by which one best represents the 2019 seed-dispersal study.

whyCorrect: The colon spells out what the exchange does: it connects small Cambodian companies to knowledgeable investors and thereby "can help those companies thrive." The blank needs a verb meaning to support something so it can grow, which is what "nurture" means.

whyWrong.A: "Designate" means to assign a name or official status, which is not what connecting companies to investors accomplishes.
whyWrong.C: "Preclude" means to prevent, the opposite of helping the companies thrive.
whyWrong.D: "Assess" means to evaluate; the exchange is described as supporting the companies, not judging them.

tips: The clause after the colon is a definition of the blank — turn it into a single verb before reading the choices.

whyCorrect: The example after the colon is about how often a password was used: "abc123" was the fifth most commonly used password of 2013. That measures how widespread a choice is, so the blank describes the approach most people actually take, which favors convenience over the complexity developers recommend.

whyWrong.A: "Complex" describes what developers urge; the sentence's "Nonetheless" signals that real behavior runs the other way, toward easy passwords.
whyWrong.B: "Useful" says nothing about frequency, and the example measures how many people used the password, not how well it worked.
whyWrong.C: "Creative" contradicts the example — "abc123" is the least creative password imaginable.

commonMistakes: Picking "complex" by echoing the first sentence; "Nonetheless" tells you the blank contrasts with what developers encourage.

whyCorrect: The first sentence sets the logic: lessons from past biodiversity declines can inform policy for species at risk now. The second sentence applies that to a specific case — the causes of an ancient extinction may carry over to species endangered today. "Applicable to" is the phrase for one thing being relevant to another.

whyWrong.A: "Concealed from" would mean the factors are hidden from today's species, which reverses the point that past lessons are useful now.
whyWrong.C: "Integrated with" suggests the old factors are being combined into the species themselves, which makes no sense for causes of extinction.
whyWrong.D: "Dependent on" makes the ancient factors rely on modern endangered species, backwards in time and in logic.

tips: Notice the direction of the relationship: past causes inform present cases, so the blank must point from the old factors toward today's species.

whyCorrect: The sentence explains why turnover is hard to fight: sellers must add "other incentives to bolster retention" because the customer's original enthusiasm does not last. The blank therefore needs a verb meaning to fade or die down, and "subside" is that verb.

whyWrong.B: "Rejuvenate" means to be renewed, which would mean enthusiasm keeps refreshing itself and no extra incentives would be needed.
whyWrong.C: "Converge" means to come together at a point and cannot describe a feeling weakening.
whyWrong.D: "Resolve" means to settle or decide something; enthusiasm is not a dispute or a problem to be resolved.

tips: When the sentence says sellers must compensate for something, the blank names the thing going wrong — here, enthusiasm dropping off.

whyCorrect: "In short" means the last sentence restates the two claims before it: that public understanding of history is central to comprehending politics, and that historical issues cannot belong to experts alone. The second half of the sentence already carries the experts point, so the blank has to carry the first — that historical knowledge is not unnecessary for ordinary citizens. "Superfluous" means unnecessary, so "not superfluous" states exactly that.

whyWrong.A: "Unattainable" would claim the passage argued that ordinary people can acquire historical knowledge, but the argument is about why they need it, not whether they can get it.
whyWrong.C: "Not commonplace" would say historical knowledge is rare, which does not summarize either claim and clashes with the call for widespread public understanding.
whyWrong.D: "Equitable" describes fairness of distribution, a property the passage never assigns to knowledge itself.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that "In short" requires the sentence to summarize both earlier claims, not just repeat the one about experts.

whyCorrect: The conclusion is that the birds react to T. caesius alarm calls specifically because they read them as danger. The obvious hole is that they might freeze or scatter at any sudden sound. A control showing no reaction to random noise closes that hole, leaving the alarm call itself as what triggers the response.

whyWrong.A: Shows the birds reacting to the approaching researchers rather than to any playback, which offers a rival explanation for the freezing and undercuts the conclusion.
whyWrong.C: Says other species react the same way; that broadens who responds but adds nothing about why S. leucostigma does.
whyWrong.D: Consistency across different callers rules out an individual-caller effect, but the birds could still be reacting to loud sound in general rather than to danger.

tips: For a "most directly supports" question, ask what alternative explanation is still open, then pick the finding that eliminates it.

whyCorrect: The proposal is that a high metabolic rate is what let birds survive while other dinosaurs died. To undermine it you need a case where high metabolism did not protect an animal from this extinction. Dinosaurs with very high metabolic rates dying out 65 million years ago is exactly that case: it breaks the link between the trait and survival.

whyWrong.A: Declining metabolisms in non-avian dinosaurs would fit the proposal, since it makes them less metabolically capable than birds.
whyWrong.B: Suggests some non-avian dinosaurs had high rates but stops at an inference from movement speed and never says what happened to them, so the survival link stays intact.
whyWrong.C: Confirms that birds have very high metabolisms, which supports the proposal rather than weakening it.

tips: To weaken a "trait X caused survival" claim, look for cases that had trait X and still died.

whyCorrect: The belief being challenged is that people everywhere map time onto an imagined straight axis fixed to the body, like the Spanish speakers' left-to-right line. Yupno speakers instead gesture according to the terrain: uphill for the future, so the same future points in front of them or behind them depending on which way they face. A time mapping that flips with the landscape is not a body-based linear axis, which is what Núñez needs to show the tendency is not universal.

whyWrong.A: Compares indoor and outdoor gesture frequency, which says nothing about the direction time is mapped onto.
whyWrong.C: Using one hand for both past and future gestures shows no directional distinction at all, so it neither confirms nor refutes an axis-based mapping.
whyWrong.D: Shared grammatical structures with Spanish would suggest similarity between the two languages, pointing toward universality rather than against it.

commonMistakes: Treating any fact about Yupno gestures as support; the finding has to show a time mapping that is not a fixed linear axis.

whyCorrect: Track where the Round Table could have come from. Malory drew heavily on Geoffrey's History, but neither History nor anything written before it mentions the Round Table, while Malory's book does. So the detail cannot have reached him through Geoffrey or through Geoffrey's own sources; it must have come from somewhere Geoffrey could not have known when he wrote in the 1130s.

whyWrong.A: Concerns which version Malory picked when sources conflicted, but the Round Table is missing from History entirely — there is no competing version to prefer.
whyWrong.B: Raises historical accuracy, which the text never evaluates, and its reasoning about publication dates does not bear on the Round Table at all.
whyWrong.C: Compares overall similarity among three texts, a broad claim the single Round Table detail cannot support.

tips: With "neither X nor anything before X mentions it," the inference is almost always about where else the detail could have come from.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence states the limitation: a flat photograph cannot show how a building complements, blends with, or clashes with what is around it. So the conclusion about an image of the Leaning Tower must be that it leaves out part of what the building actually does — it cannot deliver the building's full effect, only a partial view of it.

whyWrong.A: Introduces deterioration of materials, a topic the text never raises; the limitation described is about surroundings, not decay.
whyWrong.B: Says the image inflates the tower's historical importance, but nothing in the text suggests photographs overstate anything.
whyWrong.C: Shifts to how non-visitors perceive the building, whereas the passage is about what the photograph itself cannot capture — and it is architects, not tourists, who are described looking at it.

commonMistakes: Choosing an option that sounds critical of photographs generally; the conclusion has to follow from the specific limitation the text names.

whyCorrect: Strip out the dashes and the subject is "many works featured in the show," which is plural. The material between the dashes — the Duchamp painting — is an aside and never changes the number of the verb. "At the time" also fixes the tense as past, so the verb must be "were."

whyWrong.B: "Was" agrees with the singular noun inside the dashes rather than with the actual subject, "many works."
whyWrong.C: "Is" is both singular and present, clashing with the plural subject and with "at the time."
whyWrong.D: "Has been" is singular and present perfect, describing something continuing into now, which contradicts "at the time."

tips: Cross out everything between paired dashes or commas, then check subject-verb agreement on what is left.

whyCorrect: The end of the text — "the exhibition showcases the diverse, innovative, often aesthetically daring work of female photographers" — is a complete sentence with its own subject and verb. The words before it also form a complete sentence about where Horna's photograph is collected, so the two must be separated by a period. That leaves "Featuring works by artists from over twenty countries" as an opening modifier attached to "the exhibition."

whyWrong.A: A comma cannot join two independent clauses, so "Camera, featuring... , the exhibition showcases..." is a splice.
whyWrong.C: Attaching "featuring" directly to the title still leaves one complete sentence running into another with only a comma.
whyWrong.D: "and featuring" tries to coordinate a participle with the earlier verb and still leaves the second independent clause spliced on.

commonMistakes: This item's blank was transcribed in the wrong spot — the word "Camera" belongs at the end of the exhibition title, The New Woman Behind the Camera — so read the sentence with the choice inserted there.

whyCorrect: An em dash already opens the interruption before "through community involvement and scientific study," and punctuation that sets off an aside has to match at both ends. Only a second em dash closes what the first one opened, letting the sentence resume with "aims to bring adjutants back from near extinction."

whyWrong.B: Mixes marks — a dash on one side and a comma on the other — so the interrupting phrase is never properly closed.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete sentence and introduce what comes after, but here the sentence is mid-interruption and has not reached its verb.
whyWrong.D: Leaves the opening dash unmatched, so the aside runs into the rest of the clause with no boundary at all.

tips: When you see one dash before the blank, look for a dash among the choices first — paired marks must be the same kind.

whyCorrect: The sentence's only main verb is "is," and it links Yerevan to two things joined by "and": "the capital city of Armenia" and "home to an impressive 36 percent of Armenia's total population." The material between the commas is an aside, so it needs a participle rather than a second finite verb. "Containing roughly one million people" is that participial phrase.

whyWrong.A: "Contained" reads as a past-tense verb dropped into an interrupting phrase, leaving the clause with two competing main verbs.
whyWrong.B: "Contains" is a finite verb, so the phrase inside the commas becomes a clause that the sentence has no way to attach.
whyWrong.D: "Has contained" is likewise finite and adds a present-perfect tense that clashes with the simple present "is."

tips: If a phrase is fenced off by commas in the middle of a clause, it usually cannot carry a tensed verb.

whyCorrect: The sentence is about two places — Arteaga and Lagos de Moreno — so the noun must be plural, and "these" confirms it. The natural beauty and traditions belong to those towns, so the plural noun also has to be possessive: "towns'" with the apostrophe after the s.

whyWrong.A: "Town" is singular and not possessive, so it neither matches "these" nor shows ownership of the beauty and traditions.
whyWrong.B: "Town's" is possessive but singular, contradicting "these" and the two named towns.
whyWrong.C: "Towns" is correctly plural but has no apostrophe, so it cannot show that the beauty and traditions belong to them.

tips: Decide plural or singular first, then add the apostrophe — plural possessives put it after the s.

whyCorrect: "The liquid compound" does not tell you which compound, so "dodecane (C12H26)" is essential information and takes no commas. With the name attached directly, the subject runs straight into its verb "has," which is what Standard English requires.

whyWrong.A: Sets the name off with paired commas, treating it as skippable extra information when the sentence needs it to identify the compound.
whyWrong.B: Opens with a comma after "compound" but never closes the aside before "has," so the punctuation is unpaired.
whyWrong.C: Puts a single comma between the full subject and the verb "has," a break that is never allowed.

commonMistakes: Assuming a name in the middle of a sentence always gets commas; commas depend on whether the sentence already identifies the thing.

whyCorrect: The first sentence is set in 1929, when scientists believed progesterone existed only in animals. The second says the corn-plant discovery "wouldn't come until decades later." The transition has to mark that long gap in time, and "Eventually" does exactly that.

whyWrong.A: "In other words" signals a restatement, but finding progesterone in plants is new information that overturns the earlier assumption.
whyWrong.B: "For example" would make the corn discovery an instance of the animals-only assumption, when it is the counterexample to it.
whyWrong.D: "Earlier" puts the discovery before 1929, directly contradicting "this discovery wouldn't come until decades later."

tips: When the sentence itself contains a time cue like "decades later," the transition must agree with it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the broad aim — analyzing the cattle's diet composition. The second narrows it to a precise version of the same aim: the ratio among graminoids, forbs, and browse. Moving from a general goal to its detailed form calls for "Specifically."

whyWrong.A: "Instead" would mean the second aim replaced the first, but it is the first aim stated in finer detail.
whyWrong.B: "All the same" concedes something despite an obstacle, and there is no tension between the two sentences.
whyWrong.C: "Therefore" claims the second aim is a consequence of the first; it is a refinement of it, not a result.

tips: A colon-led list of subtypes right after a general statement is a strong sign the transition is narrowing, not contrasting.

whyCorrect: Before the blank, an information cascade helps the group — fish copy their school-mates and escape a predator. After it, the same copying spreads false alarms and drives sandpipers off safe nesting grounds. The blank sits between a benefit and a harm produced by the same mechanism, so it needs a contrast word, and "Conversely" marks the flip.

whyWrong.A: "In other words" promises a restatement, but the sandpiper case reverses the outcome instead of rephrasing the fish case.
whyWrong.C: "Indeed" strengthens the point just made; here the second sentence pushes against it rather than confirming it.
whyWrong.D: "Consequently" claims the misinformation problem is caused by the beneficial cascade, but the two studies present opposite outcomes, not cause and effect.

tips: When one sentence says "benefits" and the next says "unfavorable results," the transition is doing contrast work.

whyCorrect: A difference sentence has to name both novels and state the point on which they diverge. This choice does that directly: both are epistolary, but one is built from letters and the other from journal entries. That is the only contrast the notes actually record between the two books.

whyWrong.A: Names both authors but says only that each wrote an epistolary novel — a shared trait, not a difference.
whyWrong.C: Makes a claim the notes never support, that most epistolary novels use letters, and it leaves Creech's novel unnamed.
whyWrong.D: Mentions both novels but frames them as jointly illustrating variety in the form, which emphasizes the category rather than how the two differ.

commonMistakes: Accepting a choice that hints at variety; a difference sentence must put the two items side by side on the same feature.

whyCorrect: The goal is a similarity between the two artworks, so the sentence must name both works and give something they share. Both Lady in Brown and Mobile: Pittsburgh won Carnegie Prize gold medals, and this choice states exactly that.

whyWrong.B: Covers only Lavery and Lady in Brown, so there is no second artwork to compare it with.
whyWrong.C: Is about the museum's record of awarding medals across media, not about the two artworks themselves.
whyWrong.D: Names both works but sets them against each other — painting versus sculpture — which is a difference, the opposite of the goal.

tips: For "similarity between two artworks," both titles must appear and the linking idea must be something true of each.

whyCorrect: Methodology means what the researchers did — the design of the experiment, not why they did it or what they found. The design here is a comparison: they tested germination in seeds that bats had eaten against seeds that bats had not. This choice describes that two-group setup and nothing else.

whyWrong.A: Reports the result of the comparison, which is a finding rather than a method.
whyWrong.C: States the research question and motivation, describing the aim rather than the procedure.
whyWrong.D: Gives outcome numbers, and it also names the wrong plant — Ficus polita instead of the Ficus obtusifolia in the notes.

commonMistakes: Confusing the study's purpose with its methodology; "wanted to explore" signals aim, "tested" signals method.

whyCorrect: The example after the colon describes a loop: coastline geography shapes where sediment is deposited, and that deposition then reshapes the coastline. Each factor both affects and is affected by the other, so the blank needs a word for mutual reliance — "interdependent."

whyWrong.A: "Tenuous" means weak or flimsy, but the example shows factors with strong, lasting effects on each other.
whyWrong.C: "Unyielding" means unchanging, which contradicts an example in which the coastline is continually altered.
whyWrong.D: "Comprehensive" means covering everything; it describes coverage, not the relationship between the factors that the example lays out.

tips: When the example runs in a circle — A changes B, B changes A — the blank is about mutual influence.

whyCorrect: The second sentence gives the reason: most of the sculptures were moved from where they were found, and that makes "precise dating impossible." If precision is out of reach, the dates can only be rough estimates, so "approximate" is the word the blank needs.

whyWrong.A: "Uncontroversial" says nobody disputes the dates, but the loss of original context makes them less certain, not more agreed upon.
whyWrong.B: "Irrelevant" would mean the dates do not matter at all, an overstatement — archaeologists still assign them.
whyWrong.C: "Applicable" says the dates are usable but tells you nothing about their precision, which is the point the second sentence makes.

tips: The word "necessarily" signals that the second sentence will explain what forces the blank's quality — read it first.

whyCorrect: The second sentence defines the blank: "new batteries can't be put in once the old ones no longer work." Putting a new battery in place of a dead one is replacing it, so the blank has to say the batteries cannot easily be replaced.

whyWrong.A: "Invented" concerns creating a technology for the first time, not swapping a dead battery in a device someone already owns.
whyWrong.B: "Prevented" would mean stopping the batteries from existing or acting, which does not describe anything in the second sentence.
whyWrong.C: "Rated" means assigned a measurement or grade, and nothing here is about evaluating the batteries.

tips: When the following sentence paraphrases the blank in plain words, translate that paraphrase into one verb before scanning the choices.

whyCorrect: The word "conversely" between the two options tells you the blank must be the opposite of "historically significant." "Inconsequential" means having little importance or effect, which is that opposite.

whyWrong.A: "Momentous" is a synonym for historically significant, so it repeats the first option instead of reversing it.
whyWrong.C: "Benevolent" describes a ruler's kindness, a different quality altogether from historical importance.
whyWrong.D: "Genuine" concerns authenticity; a reign's authenticity is not the flip side of its significance.

tips: "Or, conversely," is an instruction to supply an antonym of the word just used.

whyCorrect: The second sentence calls the Heaney and Lambert portraits "characteristic works" and "esteemed," which means Edwards is both known for and admired for painting portraits of notable people. "A reputation for" is the phrase that captures being widely known for doing something.

whyWrong.B: "Requirement for" would mean he is obligated to paint such portraits, but nothing suggests he has no choice.
whyWrong.C: "Complaint about" turns his best-known work into a grievance, contradicting "esteemed."
whyWrong.D: "Question about" implies doubt or inquiry, while the sentence describes an established body of admired work.

tips: Words like "esteemed" and "characteristic" point to how the artist is regarded, so the blank should be about reputation.

whyCorrect: The conclusion is that the flycatchers react to the antshrike's alarm calls specifically, treating them as a signal of danger. The competing explanation is that they startle at any sudden sound. A control in which random noise produced no reaction removes that explanation and leaves the alarm call itself as the trigger.

whyWrong.A: Reports that other species react the same way, which says nothing about why M. barbatus does.
whyWrong.B: Shows the response does not depend on which individual antshrike called, but the birds could still be reacting to loud noise in general.
whyWrong.C: Describes birds reacting to the approaching researchers rather than to the playback, which supplies a rival cause and weakens the conclusion.

tips: A control condition is the classic support for "the response was caused by this stimulus" claims.

whyCorrect: The claim is about a turning point: Mère Poussepin marks a significant change in John's development. Support therefore has to show her work before that painting differing from her work after it. This quotation does exactly that — the earlier paintings form a style she abandoned and never came back to, which puts the break at that painting.

whyWrong.A: Describes disagreement among viewers about the painting's meaning, which is about interpretation, not about a change in the artist's development.
whyWrong.B: Ranks the painting as her fullest expression of her abilities, but being her best work does not mean her work changed after it.
whyWrong.D: Says she was ahead of her time and influenced by contemporaries, a claim about her place among other artists rather than about a shift in her own career.

commonMistakes: Treating high praise for the painting as evidence of change; the claim needs a before-and-after, not a superlative.

whyCorrect: The conclusion has two parts: people really can tell the two kinds of laughter apart, and they can do it everywhere. A 64% success rate is well above the 50% you would get by guessing, which establishes the ability; similar rates in Austria, Samoa, and the other societies establishes that it holds across cultures. Only this finding delivers both parts.

whyWrong.A: Ties judgments to societies' economic conditions, which makes the ability vary with culture — the opposite of universal.
whyWrong.C: Reports acoustic variation in the laughs themselves, a fact about the stimuli that says nothing about whether listeners judged them correctly.
whyWrong.D: Covers only two of the twenty-one societies and reports no differences without ever showing that listeners judged accurately; people could be equally poor everywhere.

tips: For a universality claim, check that the evidence shows both accuracy and breadth — one without the other leaves the conclusion unsupported.

whyCorrect: The key sentence says that in every class of animals — amphibians included — there were individual studies with differences well above the mammal average. A number above the mammal average has to be above at least some of the individual mammal results that produced that average. So some amphibian studies must have found larger effects than some mammal studies did.

whyWrong.B: Brings in whether studies specified that effects were detrimental, something the passage never reports.
whyWrong.C: Turns individual high-scoring amphibian studies into a general rule that amphibians are affected more, contradicting the stated fact that mammal studies showed larger differences on average.
whyWrong.D: Compares Shier's study to an average for Stephens kangaroo rat studies, a figure the passage never gives and a comparison the meta-analysis never makes.

commonMistakes: Sliding from "some studies exceeded the average" to "this group is affected more" — an average and an individual study are different claims.

whyCorrect: Tarabieh's relationship runs in one direction: the higher the perceived environmental risk, the lower the likelihood of buying. The China study found that rural residents perceived the highest environmental risk in the TV of any group. Feed that into Tarabieh's relationship and the group with the highest perceived risk should be the least likely to buy.

whyWrong.A: Reverses the direction — high perceived risk predicts less appeal, not more — and drags in rival products neither study examined.
whyWrong.B: Claims rural residents weigh other factors above sustainability, but the study measured how much risk they perceived, not what they prioritize.
whyWrong.C: Says the groups are essentially alike, contradicting the finding that rural residents stood at the top of the risk-perception range.

tips: State the first study as a direction, then plug the second study's extreme group into it before reading any choice.

whyCorrect: Each half of this sentence is complete on its own: "In Antarctica, the Syowa East observatory site monitors activity in the upper atmosphere of the southern hemisphere" and "in Finland, another observatory site, Hankasalmi, monitors the sky of the northern hemisphere." Two independent clauses need a semicolon or a period between them, and the semicolon is the only such mark offered.

whyWrong.A: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: "And" can join two independent clauses only with a comma before it; "hemisphere and in Finland" has none.
whyWrong.D: No punctuation at all runs the two clauses together.

tips: Cover the blank and read each side aloud — if both could end with a period, a comma is not enough.

whyCorrect: The blank is the second verb in the relative clause "which typically are woven from sumac and ___ bold colors." It has to match "are woven" — same subject ("which," standing for the baskets), same present tense. "Feature" is the plural present form that keeps the pair parallel.

whyWrong.B: "Had featured" is past perfect, placing the action before some earlier past event that the sentence never establishes.
whyWrong.C: "Were featuring" shifts to past progressive, clashing with the present-tense "are woven" and with "is apparent."
whyWrong.D: "Featured" is simple past, breaking the parallel with the present-tense verb it is joined to by "and."

tips: When "and" links two verbs with one subject, check that both carry the same tense and number.

whyCorrect: "Kizomba... has become an international phenomenon" is a complete sentence, and so is "In 2022, the Indian dance duo known as Elvis and Namrata defeated performers from around the world..." Two complete sentences require a period between them, with "In" starting the second one.

whyWrong.A: Runs "phenomenon in 2022, the Indian dance duo..." together, leaving one sentence colliding with the next.
whyWrong.B: Uses only a comma between two independent clauses — a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: "and" without a preceding comma cannot join two independent clauses, and the result reads as though the phenomenon happened "and in 2022."

commonMistakes: Reading "in 2022" as part of the first clause; the date belongs to the sentence about the duo's win.

whyCorrect: The relative pronoun "which" stands for "Kansas City International Airport," a single airport, so the verb must be singular. The airport's location is a permanent, present fact, so the simple present "is" is the right tense even though the passenger figures are from the past.

whyWrong.B: "Are" is plural and cannot agree with the single airport that "which" refers to.
whyWrong.C: "Were" is both plural and past, disagreeing in number and needlessly putting a permanent location in the past.
whyWrong.D: "Have been" is plural present perfect, again failing to agree with the singular subject.

tips: Trace "which" back to the noun right before it, then match the verb to that noun.

whyCorrect: The sentence's subject is "The terms" and its verb is "illustrate"; everything in between is extra information. That extra information opens with the comma after "terms," so it has to close with a matching comma after the book's title before the sentence moves on to "such as 'karst.'"

whyWrong.B: A colon must follow a complete sentence, and "The terms, included in... Home Ground: A Guide to the American Landscape" has not reached its verb yet.
whyWrong.C: An em dash cannot close an aside that a comma opened; the two ends must match.
whyWrong.D: Leaves the aside unclosed, so the modifier runs into "such as 'karst'" with no boundary.

tips: Find the subject and its verb first; whatever sits between them is an interruption, and its punctuation must be symmetrical.

whyCorrect: "The mechanism by which plants use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into nutrients" is an appositive renaming "Photosynthesis," and it opened with a comma. It has to close with a comma too, so the main verb "is fueled" can attach to the subject "Photosynthesis."

whyWrong.A: Provides no closing punctuation, so the appositive collides with the main verb.
whyWrong.B: "And" would coordinate the appositive with the verb phrase "is fueled," two things that cannot be joined.
whyWrong.D: An em dash cannot close an aside that began with a comma; the marks must be a matched pair.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that the comma after "Photosynthesis" already opened something that must be closed.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the situation — millions of trips a year depend on the Metro. The second gives what officials do about it: maintain all 71 stations so those journeys go smoothly. The maintenance is a response to the heavy reliance, so the transition needs to show cause leading to action.

whyWrong.B: "However" signals a reversal, but the second sentence follows from the first rather than opposing it.
whyWrong.C: "For example" would make station maintenance an instance of residents taking trips, which it is not.
whyWrong.D: "Alternatively" offers a competing option, and no options are being weighed here.

tips: If the second sentence describes a response to the first, look for a cause-and-effect transition.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the two volcanoes look alike from a distance. The second says specialists can tell they are different types entirely. That is a reversal of the impression just given, so the interrupter needs to be a contrast word — "though."

whyWrong.A: "For example" would make the volcanologists' expert judgment an instance of the volcanoes looking similar, which reverses the relationship.
whyWrong.B: "In addition" adds a similar point, but the second sentence undercuts the first rather than piling on.
whyWrong.C: "Therefore" claims the expert distinction follows from the resemblance, when it works against it.

tips: A transition dropped between commas mid-sentence still has to carry the logic — read the two sentences as a pair first.

whyCorrect: Hayden's poem meditates on a Monet painting, and Alexander's poem does the same thing with an Agnes Martin painting. Both are being offered as parallel examples of ekphrastic poetry, so the transition has to signal "in the same way" — that is "likewise."

whyWrong.A: "Conversely" announces an opposite, but the second poem behaves exactly like the first.
whyWrong.B: "Nevertheless" concedes something despite an obstacle, and there is no obstacle in the first example.
whyWrong.C: "Hence" claims Alexander's poem is a consequence of Hayden's, but they are simply two independent examples.

commonMistakes: Treating the second example as a contrast because it involves a different poet and painting; a second instance of the same pattern calls for an additive transition.

whyCorrect: The goal is to describe a color popular at 2019 New York Fashion Week, so the sentence has to name that event and describe the color itself. Only this choice does both, giving the shade as warm in tone, rich in intensity, and deep brown.

whyWrong.A: Mentions both colors and both events but describes neither shade beyond its name, and it never singles out New York 2019.
whyWrong.B: Spends its description on the London green-yellow shade and defines the New York color only as a departure from it, so the brown itself is never described.
whyWrong.C: Explains what color consultants do; it names no color and no specific Fashion Week.

tips: When the goal says "describe a color," the sentence needs actual descriptive words — tone, intensity, hue — not just a comparison.

whyCorrect: Two conditions have to be met: the sentence must report what the study found, and it must not waste words explaining seedling emergence to readers who already know the term. This choice gives the finding — plant litter had a positive effect on seedling emergence in that grassland setting — and skips the definition.

whyWrong.A: Gives only the publication year and reports no finding at all.
whyWrong.B: States the finding but then defines seedling emergence, which the specified audience already understands.
whyWrong.C: Says the topic has been studied and defines plant litter, without reporting any result.

tips: An "audience already familiar with X" instruction is telling you to eliminate the choice that defines X.

whyCorrect: A definition states what the term means, and the notes define it in one line: a river with high sinuosity has many meanders. This choice gives exactly that and adds the short gloss of "meander" as a U-shaped curve, so a reader who knows neither term walks away with both.

whyWrong.B: Adds how meanders change shape and migrate, which describes their behavior over time rather than defining what makes a river high-sinuosity.
whyWrong.C: Explains how meanders form through erosion and redeposition — a causal mechanism, not a definition of the term.
whyWrong.D: Describes what will happen to one particular river, the Willapa, instead of defining the category.

commonMistakes: Choosing the most detailed option; a definition should give the defining feature, not every related fact.

whyCorrect: The relative clause says Southerland's book was among the presenter's favorites as a child, and the presenter credits her inspiration to it. The blank therefore names a positive attachment to that work, and "an affinity for" means exactly a natural liking for something.

whyWrong.B: "A stipulation about" is a condition or requirement, which has nothing to do with being inspired by a book.
whyWrong.C: "An ambivalence toward" means mixed feelings, contradicting "among the presenter's favorite books."
whyWrong.D: "A complacency about" means self-satisfied unconcern, the opposite of the motivation the presenter describes.

tips: When a sentence says someone credits their inspiration to something, the blank has to be positive.

whyCorrect: The semicolon introduces the evidence: subjects' eyes went to where the target ball would have gone if the other ball had not existed. That is imagining an alternative to what actually happened, which is what "counterfactual" thinking means.

whyWrong.B: "Analogical" thinking maps one situation onto a similar one, but subjects were imagining a different version of the same event, not a parallel case.
whyWrong.C: "Ambivalent" describes mixed feelings and cannot describe a mode of causal reasoning about billiard balls.
whyWrong.D: "Associative" thinking links things that occur together; the eye-tracking shows subjects modeling an event that never occurred at all.

tips: The phrase "would have gone if... did not exist" is the giveaway — that construction is the grammar of a counterfactual.

whyCorrect: The dash spells out the meaning: "other economists clearly find her studies valuable for their own scholarship." So the frequent citations confirm and emphasize the usefulness of her research. "Underscores" is the verb for highlighting or reinforcing a point.

whyWrong.A: "Overshadows" means to obscure or outshine, but the citations reveal her work's usefulness rather than hiding it.
whyWrong.C: "Belies" means to contradict or give a false impression of, the reverse of the confirming relationship the dash spells out.
whyWrong.D: "Forestalls" means to prevent in advance, which cannot apply to a quality that the citations demonstrate.

tips: Read past the dash before choosing — it usually restates the blank in plain terms.

whyCorrect: Trofimov lists hardships — hunger, illness, being shaken, tossed everywhere by fate — so "a great deal" refers to suffering he has lived through. "Undergone" here means to have gone through and withstood, which is "endured."

whyWrong.A: "Neglected" would mean he ignored these hardships, but the whole speech insists he has experienced them.
whyWrong.B: "Enjoyed" reverses the tone of a list built on hunger and illness.
whyWrong.C: "Conveyed" means communicated to someone, but he is describing what happened to him, not what he passed along.

tips: For a word-in-context item in a passage of complaint, let the surrounding list of details set the emotional register.

whyCorrect: The realists are described as accurately portraying ordinary working life, and the romantic style is set against that by the word "instead." The rest of the clause says romantic paintings hide all imperfection, so the blank must describe the flattering half of that treatment: playing up the subjects' beauty or heroism. "Accentuate" means to emphasize or heighten.

whyWrong.A: "Counteract" means to work against, so it would have the paintings suppressing the beauty they are said to display.
whyWrong.C: "Rectify" means to correct a fault, but beauty and heroism are not faults needing repair.
whyWrong.D: "Obscure" means to hide — that is what the paintings do to imperfection, not to beauty and heroism.

commonMistakes: Grabbing "obscure" because "hiding" appears later in the sentence; the two halves of the clause do opposite things to different qualities.

whyCorrect: The claim is that a steady energy load is an absolute prerequisite for powering wireless communication devices piezoelectrically. To support that, you need evidence that unsteady power actually breaks such devices. The finding that intermittent or unpredictable supply undermines their efficacy establishes exactly why steadiness is required.

whyWrong.A: Says ordinary non-CFRP harvesters already suffice, which undercuts the need for the new steady-output design rather than supporting the claim about steadiness.
whyWrong.C: Incompatibility with wireless devices would make the new harvester useless for them, working against the claim.
whyWrong.D: Attributes sufficient output to the electrode's conductivity, which is about the quantity of energy, not about the steadiness the claim rests on.

tips: Identify the exact word the claim hangs on — here "steady" — and pick the finding that explains why that property matters.

whyCorrect: The hypothesis predicts a pattern: the farther a population moved from Africa through successive splits, the fewer sounds its language kept. Support therefore needs a pair of regions where the one closer to Africa has more sounds. Eastern Europe is closer to Africa than East Asia and its languages have more sounds, which is the predicted direction.

whyWrong.A: Puts more sounds in the region farther from Africa, the reverse of what the hypothesis predicts.
whyWrong.C: Has the region closer to Africa carrying fewer sounds, which runs directly against the hypothesis.
whyWrong.D: Compares two regions at roughly the same distance from Africa, so the sound difference cannot be explained by distance either way.

tips: Turn the hypothesis into a rule — farther means fewer — then test each pair against it before reading the wording closely.

whyCorrect: The study is meant to compare the effects of different conservation strategies, and the way you would see an effect is a rise or fall in the langur population. The text says counting these primates accurately is hard, so researchers cannot tell whether the population is growing, shrinking, or holding steady. Without a reliable population figure, any judgment about which strategy is working could be wrong.

whyWrong.B: Predicts other conservationists will change their counting methods, but the text never says a better method exists or is being developed.
whyWrong.C: Suggests widening the study to other species, which does nothing about the counting problem the text raises.
whyWrong.D: Concerns which strategies are included in the study, while the stated difficulty is measuring outcomes, not choosing strategies.

tips: When a passage names a measurement problem, the conclusion is usually about what that problem does to the study's results.

whyCorrect: The researchers knew soil moisture varies in the wild and could itself change plant chemistry, so it would confound any result. By potting the plants individually in a controlled environment, they held moisture constant and varied only the microbial communities. That design lets them attribute any differences in glucosinolates to the microbes rather than to moisture.

whyWrong.B: Frames moisture as something the microbes influence, but the text treats moisture as a separate environmental variable the researchers controlled, not an effect of the microbial communities.
whyWrong.C: Is not a completion of "enabled the researchers to" at all — it has no verb that fits the sentence — and it asserts a conclusion about flavor chemistry rather than describing what the method made possible.
whyWrong.D: Says the setup re-created wild conditions, the opposite of a controlled environment, and refers to earlier wild studies the text never mentions.

tips: When a passage names a variable that "could influence" the outcome and then describes a controlled setup, the point of the setup is to rule that variable out.

whyCorrect: "To select" needs its object, and that object is the phrase "which sites to add next to the growing registry." No punctuation may sit between a verb and the object it takes, so the blank stays empty.

whyWrong.A: A colon must follow a complete sentence, but the clause breaks off mid-infinitive before "select" has an object.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and "which sites to add next..." is not one.
whyWrong.C: A comma here cuts the verb off from its own object.

commonMistakes: Adding punctuation because the sentence is long; length never justifies breaking a verb from its object.

whyCorrect: Everything through "served in Congress" is a complete sentence, and what follows — the two names — is a list that identifies the "two other Black Americans" just mentioned. A colon is the mark that lets a complete sentence introduce a list or specification like that.

whyWrong.A: A period would leave "Josiah Thomas Walls of Florida and Thomas Ezekiel Miller of South Carolina" standing alone as a fragment with no verb.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and the pair of names is only a noun phrase.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation, the names run straight into "served in Congress," as though the men served inside those two people.

tips: A complete sentence followed by a naming list is the textbook colon situation.

whyCorrect: Read past the blank: "since the meteoroids' compression of the air surrounding them causes the vast majority to burn up in the mesosphere" begins with "since," which makes it a subordinate clause, not a second sentence. So there is only one independent clause here, and "however" is simply an interrupter inside it — it takes a comma on each side.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon demands an independent clause after it, but what follows is a "since" clause that cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.C: A period creates a second sentence out of "However, since... producing the Quadrantid meteor shower," which is a fragment with no main clause.
whyWrong.D: Puts a semicolon before a subordinate clause, the same error as A with the marks reordered.

commonMistakes: Assuming "however" always sits between two sentences; check whether the second part is actually independent before splitting it off.

whyCorrect: The sentence already has its main verb: "This hypothesis... cannot stand." So the blank cannot supply another finite verb — it has to introduce a modifier describing the hypothesis. "Suggesting that certain trees... survived without interruption" does that, leaving "cannot stand" as the predicate.

whyWrong.A: "Suggested" is a finite past verb, so the sentence ends up with two main verbs and no way to attach "cannot stand."
whyWrong.B: "Has suggested" is likewise finite and creates the same double-verb problem.
whyWrong.D: "Suggests" makes the hypothesis both suggest something and be unable to stand, with no conjunction joining the two verbs.

tips: Locate the main verb before filling any verb blank; if the sentence already has one, the blank needs a participle.

whyCorrect: The passage states a permanent scientific fact in the present tense — an atomic number "indicates" how many protons an atom has — and the example must match. "Has" is the simple present, singular to agree with "a helium atom."

whyWrong.A: "Has had" is present perfect and implies the proton count is the result of some earlier change, when it is a fixed property.
whyWrong.C: "Is having" is present progressive, which describes an action in progress and cannot describe a permanent state.
whyWrong.D: "Had" is past tense, implying helium atoms once had 2 protons but may not now.

tips: General scientific facts take the simple present, and the surrounding verbs will confirm it.

whyCorrect: The end of the text — "the transient yet powerful blast propelled particles and debris into space at extremely high speeds" — is a complete sentence with its own subject and verb. The words before it are also complete: "Named for the year in which it was detected..., SN 2020fqv was a supernova (the explosion of a massive star)." Two complete sentences need a period, which leaves "Occurring in the constellation Virgo, 60 million light-years from Earth" as an opening modifier on "the blast."
